content.text:
1) Answer

There is substantial public-record evidence that James Cleverly values human rights:

- He has repeatedly and explicitly affirmed a belief in universal human rights and the UK’s duty to defend them in office. As Foreign Secretary he wrote the preface to the FCDO’s Human Rights and Democracy Report 2022, committing to ensure “everyone can enjoy their rights,” and used Human Rights Day 2022 to state he would “work tirelessly… to promote and protect” human rights. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/human-rights-and-democracy-report-2022/human-rights-and-democracy-the-2022-foreign-commonwealth-development-office-report?utm_source=openai))

- He used UK foreign policy levers to hold abusers to account. As Foreign Secretary he announced multiple sanctions packages targeting human-rights violators, including:
  - Iran’s “morality police” and senior officials after Mahsa Amini’s death, explicitly “standing with” Iranian women and girls calling for fundamental rights. He later coordinated allied sanctions on the first anniversary. ([news.sky.com](https://news.sky.com/story/uk-sanctions-irans-morality-police-following-death-of-mahsa-amini-12717349?utm_source=openai))
  - A global package on 9 December 2022 (to mark Human Rights Day/Anti‑Corruption Day) against torturers, corrupt actors and perpetrators of conflict-related sexual violence. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-sanctions-target-30-corrupt-political-figures-human-rights-violators-and-perpetrators-of-conflict-related-sexual-violence-around-the-world?utm_source=openai))
  - Sanctions on Myanmar aviation‑fuel enablers to reduce the junta’s capacity to bomb civilians, paired with statements condemning its “brutal crackdown” and human‑rights violations. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-sanctions-myanmar-aviation-fuel-businesses-marking-two-years-since-coup?utm_source=openai))

- He put UK resources behind survivor‑centred justice. At the UK’s Preventing Sexual Violence in Conflict (PSVI) conference (Nov 2022), he launched a three‑year strategy with up to £12.5m of new funding and pledged to use sanctions specifically to address conflict‑related sexual violence. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-leads-global-action-to-tackle-sexual-violence-in-conflict?utm_source=openai))

- He advocated for human rights in multilateral fora. At the UN Human Rights Council (Feb 2023) he anchored the UK’s stance in the UDHR and rule of law, and pressed Russia to “restore human rights” at home and abroad. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/un-human-rights-council-february-2023-foreign-secretarys-statement?utm_source=openai))

- On the European Convention on Human Rights, his public position has not been to junk the treaty: in July 2025 he argued leaving the ECHR is “not [a] silver bullet,” contrasting with calls to quit it—indicating a preference to work within human‑rights frameworks rather than abandon them. ([news.sky.com](https://news.sky.com/story/james-cleverly-says-leaving-echr-is-not-silver-bullet-and-leaves-door-open-for-leadership-bid-13397044?utm_source=openai))

- Even when defending contested Home Office policies, he framed aims in human‑rights terms (e.g., in Parliament he highlighted the “fundamental” right to life when arguing deterrence to prevent deaths at sea). This shows the lens through which he justifies policy choices. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/html/commons/2023-12-06/CommonsChamber?utm_source=openai))

Taken together—consistent pro‑rights rhetoric, sanctions against abusers, funding for survivor justice, and engagement through international rights institutions—this record supports the claim that Cleverly values human rights, even if individual policies attract debate about how best to balance and protect rights in practice. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/human-rights-and-democracy-report-2022/human-rights-and-democracy-the-2022-foreign-commonwealth-development-office-report?utm_source=openai))


2) Sources I considered trustworthy

- [1] Source: GOV.UK – “Human Rights and Democracy: the 2022 FCDO report” (preface by James Cleverly)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Official UK government publication; primary record of ministerial positions and actions.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Contains Cleverly’s own signed preface setting out his human‑rights commitments. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/human-rights-and-democracy-report-2022/human-rights-and-democracy-the-2022-foreign-commonwealth-development-office-report?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: GOV.UK – “Human Rights Day 2022: Foreign Secretary’s speech”
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Primary transcript hosted by the department.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Direct, attributable statements of belief and policy on human rights by Cleverly. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/human-rights-day-2022-foreign-secretarys-speech?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: GOV.UK – “UN Human Rights Council, February 2023: Foreign Secretary’s statement”
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Official transcript; primary source.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Shows multilateral advocacy grounded in the UDHR and rule of law. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/un-human-rights-council-february-2023-foreign-secretarys-statement?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: GOV.UK – “I commend their bravery… Mahsa Amini anniversary” (UK sanctions)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Official sanctions notice; verifiable government action.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Demonstrates Cleverly’s concrete measures backing women’s rights in Iran. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/i-commend-their-bravery-foreign-secretary-recognises-bravery-of-iranian-people-on-anniversary-of-mahsa-amini-death?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: GOV.UK – “UK sanctions target 30 corrupt political figures, human rights violators…” (9 Dec 2022)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Official record of UK sanctions decisions.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Connects Cleverly personally to a large human‑rights sanctions package. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-sanctions-target-30-corrupt-political-figures-human-rights-violators-and-perpetrators-of-conflict-related-sexual-violence-around-the-world?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: GOV.UK – “UK sanctions Myanmar aviation fuel businesses marking 2 years since coup”
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Primary announcement by FCDO.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Shows use of targeted measures to mitigate human‑rights abuses against civilians. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-sanctions-myanmar-aviation-fuel-businesses-marking-two-years-since-coup?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: GOV.UK – “PSVI conference 2022: Foreign Secretary’s speech”
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Primary transcript; authoritative.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Details the £12.5m strategy and survivor‑centred commitments. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/psvi-conference-welcome-speeches-by-the-foreign-secretary-james-cleverly-and-nobel-laureate-nadia-murad-28-november-2022?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: GOV.UK – “UK leads global action to tackle sexual violence in conflict”
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Official policy/news release.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Corroborates funding and focus countries under Cleverly’s PSVI plan. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-leads-global-action-to-tackle-sexual-violence-in-conflict?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Sky News – “James Cleverly says leaving ECHR is ‘not [a] silver bullet’” (15 July 2025)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Major UK broadcaster with editorial standards and attribution.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Independent reporting of his public stance on staying within the ECHR framework. ([news.sky.com](https://news.sky.com/story/james-cleverly-says-leaving-echr-is-not-silver-bullet-and-leaves-door-open-for-leadership-bid-13397044?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Hansard (UK Parliament) – Commons Chamber, 6 Dec 2023
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Verbatim, authoritative parliamentary record.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Shows how he frames policy aims in human‑rights terms (e.g., right to life). ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/html/commons/2023-12-06/CommonsChamber?utm_source=openai))


3) Sources I considered not trustworthy

- None. For this assessment I relied on primary government records (GOV.UK, Hansard) and a mainstream UK news outlet (Sky News) with transparent sourcing; I did not include or rely on sources I judged unreliable for establishing a factual record of actions and statements.
